# Clearhead

> 1:1 coaching and counselling with Vaibhav Jain, an ICF PCC certified coach based in Mumbai. Clearhead helps professionals navigate AI-driven career anxiety, mid-career identity shifts, overwork, burnout, and loneliness — through clear, confidential conversation.

Clearhead is the private coaching practice of Vaibhav Jain (ICF PCC). Sessions are 1:1, online or in Lokhandwala, Andheri West, Mumbai, and focused on thinking clearly, being genuinely heard, and finding direction. Payments via Razorpay; booking via Cal.com.

## Core pages
- [Home — Clearhead coaching with Vaibhav Jain](https://clearhead.in/): Overview of the practice, approach, and how coaching works.
- [Pricing](https://clearhead.in/pricing.html): Session packages and rates.
- [In-Person Coaching, Andheri West](https://clearhead.in/coaching-andheri-west.html): Details on in-person sessions at Lokhandwala Complex, Andheri West, Mumbai — for Andheri, Versova, Oshiwara, and nearby.
- [Blog](https://clearhead.in/blog.html): Writing on clarity, identity, loneliness, burnout, and being heard, organized into 5 themes.

## Free interactive tools
Self-contained two-to-six-minute assessments, free, no signup required — each a standalone answer to a specific question.
- [Abundance Runway Calculator](https://clearhead.in/runway.html): How long your finances could sustain you if income stopped today.
- [Cognitive Overload / Mental Bandwidth Calculator](https://clearhead.in/bandwidth.html): Scores mental bandwidth across open loops, context switching, system dependency, and recovery.
- [Career Alignment Test](https://clearhead.in/career-friction.html): Plots where you sit — Aligned, Hard but Right, Drift, or Golden Handcuffs — and what staying costs.
- [AI Exposure / Job Replacement Calculator](https://clearhead.in/ai-relevance.html): Scores how much of your work AI can automate and what to strengthen next.
- [Self-Employment Readiness Index](https://clearhead.in/readiness.html): A six-question audit of clarity, financial stability, and risk tolerance before quitting to go solo/freelance.
- [Still On Your List](https://clearhead.in/still-on-your-list.html): A six-minute reflection on the things you've been quietly carrying and why.

## Articles — AI, work & identity
- [It isn't the fear of losing your job. It's the fear that you're no longer steering.](https://clearhead.in/post-career-insecurity.html): A 2026 study in the Journal of Business and Psychology (Fu, Wang, Guo, Xin, Hai, Han & Zhang) used three-wave data from gig and service workers to show that career insecurity, driven by AI and economic uncertainty, damages mental health and increases job withdrawal chiefly through perceived control loss, the felt loss of grip on your own path; supervisor career support mentoring buffers the effect by restoring a sense of agency. On the quiet fear behind the AI years and what actually helps.
- [AI promised your time back. Why are you busier than ever?](https://clearhead.in/post-ai-productivity-burnout.html): A 2026 Harvard Business Review study (Ranganathan & Ye) found AI does not reduce work, it intensifies it, with a faster pace, wider scope and longer hours; a 2025 Upwork survey of 2,500 workers found a 40% productivity boost but 88% burnout among the heaviest AI users, who were twice as likely to quit. On the AI productivity-burnout paradox and what helps.
- [Your job title is changing. You don't have to lose yourself with it.](https://clearhead.in/post-ai.html): The AI wave is an identity story as much as a career story.
- [You still have your job. So why does work feel less safe?](https://clearhead.in/post-ai-psychological-safety.html): A 2025 three-wave study of 381 employees (Kim, Kim & Lee, Humanities and Social Sciences Communications) found AI adoption lowers psychological safety, which in turn raises depression, even when the job is secure; ethical leadership buffers the effect.
- [The fear isn't losing the job. It's losing who you are.](https://clearhead.in/post-ai-job-fear.html): A 2025 Delphi-validated study mapped the psychological impact of AI-induced job displacement on Indian IT professionals across six stages.
- [Fear of being replaced by AI now has a clinical name.](https://clearhead.in/post-ai-replacement-dysfunction.html): A 2026 paper proposed "AI Replacement Dysfunction" (AIRD) to describe the psychological distress of facing professional obsolescence.
- [The layoff hasn't happened. Your body is already bracing.](https://clearhead.in/post-ai-job-insecurity.html): A 2025 longitudinal study found AI adoption harms mental health only through job insecurity, not directly, so the damage starts before any layoff; only 22% of workers feel safe from elimination (ADP 2026).
- [The AI you race at work follows you home.](https://clearhead.in/post-ai-work-family-exhaustion.html): A 2025 study traced a path from AI job fear to emotional exhaustion, through job insecurity, into family life.
- [Keeping up with AI is quietly exhausting you.](https://clearhead.in/post-technostress.html): A 2025 study tied AI-related technostress to measurable anxiety and depression symptoms.
- [You use AI to keep up. Is it quietly dulling your edge?](https://clearhead.in/post-ai-deskilling.html): Two 2025 studies (Gerlich in Societies; Microsoft and Carnegie Mellon) found that heavier reliance on AI lowers knowledge workers' critical thinking through cognitive offloading, and that self-confidence protects it. On AI deskilling and its toll on professional identity.
- [AI listens perfectly. It still won't cure your loneliness.](https://clearhead.in/post-ai-loneliness.html): A 2026 study found an AI chatbot rated more empathetic than a human peer — and it still didn't reduce loneliness.

## Articles — Loneliness & connection
- [Everyone reports to you. No one checks on you.](https://clearhead.in/post-lonely-at-the-top.html): Gallup's 2026 State of the Global Workplace found senior leaders score ten points higher on loneliness than the people they lead, with more daily stress, more anger and more sadness; why every promotion narrows the circle of honest feedback, plus the health and judgement cost of isolation and what actually helps.
- [Surrounded by people all day, still completely alone?](https://clearhead.in/post-workplace-loneliness-research.html): A 2026 integrated review of 233 studies in the Journal of Management finds workplace loneliness is subjective, common (about 1 in 5 workers), and structural rather than a personal failing; frequent loneliness is linked to 6.4 times higher odds of anxiety or depression.
- [The loneliest generation has the most followers.](https://clearhead.in/post-lonely.html): The most connected and most lonely generation — more ways to be heard, fewer people who listen.
- [You run the room. So why do you feel so alone in it?](https://clearhead.in/post-lonely-at-work.html): A 2025 prospective study found workplace loneliness predicted which employees left their jobs six months later.
- [Alone all day at work, even with a full life at home?](https://clearhead.in/post-alone-at-work.html): A 2025 study of 5,400 employees found workplace loneliness barely overlaps with personal loneliness and independently raises the odds of depression, anxiety and absenteeism, hitting managers hardest.
- [Moved cities for a job? The loneliness is real.](https://clearhead.in/post-new-city-loneliness.html): The quiet loneliness that arrives six months after relocating for work.
- [You can be indispensable and still feel invisible.](https://clearhead.in/post-mattering-at-work.html): New research on "mattering" finds feeling uncounted at work, separate from overwork, predicts anxiety and depression.

## Articles — Clarity & being heard
- [What one good conversation can do.](https://clearhead.in/post-conversation.html): You say something, and somewhere in the middle of it, you hear yourself say something you didn't know you thought.
- [You're not confused. You're just unheard.](https://clearhead.in/post-unheard.html): Most people who think they don't know what they want actually do — they just haven't said it out loud to someone listening.

## Articles — Pressure & burnout
- [You're not overworked. You're underused. And it shows.](https://clearhead.in/post-underused-at-work.html): Being underused, or skills-based underemployment, means working in a role that draws on far less of your skill, experience and judgment than you have; it is distinct from having too little to do, because you can be busy all week and still be underused. A 2025 longitudinal study of 18,285 working-age Australians across 21 waves of the HILDA survey (2002 to 2022), measured with the MHI-5 scale (Health Promotion International, 40(2), 10.1093/heapro/daaf030), found both hours-based and skills-based underemployment were tied to worse mental health over time, with skills-based underuse the stronger factor for men. Researchers explain it through relative deprivation and latent deprivation theory: a job is meant to supply purpose, status and identity, and underuse quietly withholds them while the pay stays intact. It lands hardest on capable, career-invested people, because a 2018 study in the Journal of Vocational Behavior found perceived overqualification turns into deprivation and lower wellbeing most strongly when career matters most, and because competence works as camouflage that keeps the struggle invisible. What helps: name the gap between your capacity and your role (Career Friction & Alignment Audit), rebuild autonomy so you can stretch the work yourself (job autonomy buffers the harm, Social Indicators Research 2014), find a real sense of a path forward (a 2026 Applied Psychology study found visible career opportunity softens the same overqualification), test whether you have outgrown the role (Self-Employment Readiness Index), and say it out loud instead of filing it under ingratitude.
- [It's not the hours. It's that you can't put it down.](https://clearhead.in/post-workaholism.html): Workaholism (work addiction) is not working hard, it is a compulsion to work with a loss of control that continues even when it harms health, mood, and relationships; the tell is not hours worked but the anxiety, guilt, or emptiness that appears when you stop. A 2025 four-year, two-wave study of 586 workers (Kun & Kokonyei, BMC Psychology, 13, 578, 10.1186/s40359-025-02907-6) using the Bergen Work Addiction Scale and latent class analysis found work addiction often persists chronically, and that the personal drivers of persistence were higher perfectionism, lower self-esteem, more rumination, and more external, pressure-based motivation, not the amount of work, so the engine is a belief that self-worth must be earned through output. A 2025 study of 1,233 U.S. full-time employees aged 25-65 (Tang, Frontiers in Psychology, 16, 1532636, 10.3389/fpsyg.2025.1532636) traced a serial pathway: work addiction depletes emotion regulation, which drives addictive eating as coping, which impairs physical health. The first prevalence meta-analysis of 71,625 people across 23 countries (Pallesen et al., Frontiers in Psychology, 2023, 14, 1252373, 10.3389/fpsyg.2023.1252373) put pooled workaholism at about 14 percent, roughly one in seven workers. It hits senior high achievers hardest because the workplace celebrates the pattern and their identity fuses with the role. What helps: see the always-on load (Cognitive Load & Bandwidth Index), test whether the fused role still fits (Career Friction & Alignment Audit), loosen the worth-equals-output belief through self-compassion, and talk it through.
- [You got the job you wanted. So why are you this bored?](https://clearhead.in/post-boreout.html): Boreout is chronic under-stimulation at work, the mirror image of burnout: too little challenge and meaning rather than too much. A 2024 two-wave study of 513 Finnish working adults (Li, Kaltiainen & Hakanen, BMC Public Health, 24, 907, 10.1186/s12889-024-18430-z) using latent change score modelling found that prior job boredom predicted later decreases in life satisfaction and positive functioning and later increases in anxiety and depression symptoms, with the links to anxiety and positive functioning strongest, so boredom tends to come first and then erode mental health. The term was coined by Rothlin and Werder (2007), who named three parts: boredom, being under-challenged, and loss of interest. Boreout hits capable people hardest because a role stops growing while they keep outgrowing it, and AI increasingly removes the interesting parts of a job, leaving faster but emptier work. It is distinct from laziness (the wish to do less) and from languishing (a wider flatness). What helps: separate a genuine fit problem (Career Friction & Alignment Audit) from a broader flatness, check whether the real issue is under-load rather than overload (Cognitive Load & Bandwidth Index), and talk it through.
- [You were ordered back to the office. Why does it feel like a loss?](https://clearhead.in/post-return-to-office-mandate.html): A 2026 study in Public Personnel Management (Morin, Doberstein & Charbonneau, 10.1177/00910260261444414) analysed three waves of U.S. federal workforce surveys from 2024 to 2025 after the abrupt January 2025 return-to-office mandate and found it disrupted routines, reduced employees' sense of control over their work, and introduced new emotional and logistical strains, producing an affective crisis (frustration, anger, stress), perceived performance impairment, and a loss of control (reduced autonomy and voice). This maps onto Karasek's 1979 demand-control model and a 2024 finding that persistent low job control more than doubled the risk of major depression: a mandate is a sudden cut to control on an unchanged workload. Researchers at the University of Pittsburgh (Ding, Ma, Xing, Yang & Jin, SSRN, tracking 3M+ S&P 500 employees on LinkedIn) found post-mandate turnover rose most among senior, highly skilled, and women employees, with vacancies about a quarter slower to fill, a pattern they named brain drain. The resentment is not fragility, it is what capable people feel when autonomy is removed without a conversation. What helps: measure the real cost (Cognitive Load & Bandwidth Index), tell a passing adjustment apart from a broken fit (Career Friction & Alignment Audit), and price an exit honestly (Abundance Runway Calculator) before deciding.
- [You are not tired from the work. You are tired from the face you wear.](https://clearhead.in/post-surface-acting.html): Surface acting, showing an emotion you do not feel, is the costly half of emotional labour, distinct from deep acting where you genuinely try to feel it. A 2025 study of 1,506 healthcare, care and service workers (Eriksson, Frontiers in Organizational Psychology, 3, 1628713, 10.3389/forgp.2025.1628713) used PLS-SEM serial mediation and found emotional demands drove surface acting, surface acting drove burnout (exhaustion and disengagement), and that burnout lowered mental wellbeing, with the pattern holding across professions and across every age group. A 2020 two-year prospective study of care workers (Suh & Punnett, International Archives of Occupational and Environmental Health, 94, 367-375, 10.1007/s00420-020-01585-8) found high baseline surface acting predicted the later onset of depressive symptoms, pointing the arrow from the daily faking to the low mood rather than only the reverse. The mechanism belongs to any role built on managing a face, and hits senior leaders hardest because they surface act in front of more people with fewer places to drop it. What helps: see how much of the day is surface acting rather than real work (Cognitive Load & Bandwidth Index), separate a bad stretch from a role that forces a face you no longer have (Career Friction & Alignment Audit), protect a few relationships where the mask can come off, and talk it through.
- [The meeting ended hours ago. Your mind is still in it.](https://clearhead.in/post-workplace-incivility.html): Workplace incivility is low-intensity rude or disrespectful behaviour with an ambiguous intent to harm (being talked over, a pointedly ignored message, a dismissive tone, being left off a thread), small enough to seem petty to raise, which is why it accumulates. A 2025 daily-diary study of 750 banking service employees over two weeks (Imam, Bilal & Sekiguchi, Future Business Journal, 11, 10, 10.1186/s43093-025-00437-6), using multilevel structural equation modelling and frustration-aggression theory, found supervisor incivility raised work-family conflict, partly through a spillover where the target passed the mistreatment on to co-workers and customers, so a single hostile source sours a chain and the day follows people home. A 2019 study of 699 U.S. Forest Service employees (Demsky, Fritz, Hammer & Black, Journal of Occupational Health Psychology, 24(2):228-240, 10.1037/ocp0000116) found incivility was linked to insomnia symptoms through negative work rumination (the after-hours replaying of the incident), and the harm was weakest for people with strong recovery experiences (genuine psychological detachment and relaxation) during non-work time. So the slight takes a second, the rumination takes the night, and recovery, not thicker skin, is the protective factor. It hits conscientious and senior people hardest because they absorb more and pass on less. What helps: make the invisible after-hours load visible (Cognitive Load & Bandwidth Index), tell a bad stretch apart from a role that no longer fits (Career Friction & Alignment Audit), protect real recovery time, and talk it through.
- [You never take a sick day. Showing up anyway is the costly part.](https://clearhead.in/post-presenteeism.html): A 2025 study of 27,507 workers weighted to Japan's population (Hara, Nagata, Matoba & Miyazaki, Journal of Occupational and Environmental Medicine, 67(9):699-704, 10.1097/JOM.0000000000003431) found the productivity lost to mental-health-related presenteeism, showing up while unwell, was an estimated 46.73 billion USD a year versus 1.85 billion for absenteeism, roughly 25 times more, and over seven times the country's medical costs for mental disorders. Presenteeism is the invisible, uncounted cost: still at the desk, running at half strength, for far longer than a sick day. Research in The Manchester School (Bryan, Bryce & Roberts, 2022, 10.1111/manc.12402) finds mental ill health drags work performance more than comparable physical illness. High performers are most exposed because never missing a day has become part of their identity. What helps: measure real depletion (the Cognitive Load & Bandwidth Index), separate a bad week from a misaligned job, and get an honest outside vantage point.
- [You shut the laptop hours ago. Your mind is still at the desk.](https://clearhead.in/post-hybrid-work-recovery.html): A 2026 study of 747 hybrid employees across four Italian organisations (Velati, Donati, Rubini & Miglioretti, Frontiers in Psychology, 10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1845951) found that higher remote work intensity predicted more affective rumination, the anxious, negative stewing about work that blocks recovery, but mainly among employees with lower general self-efficacy for managing their own boundaries. The number of remote days was not harmful on its own. The mechanism is lost containment: when the office no longer marks the end of the day, recovery depends on self-built boundaries and psychological detachment (Sonnentag & Fritz, 2007). The study distinguishes harmful affective rumination from harmless problem-solving pondering. Findings are correlational. Practical fixes: a fixed stop time, a commute-substitute ritual, moving the laptop out of sight, and a genuinely absorbing recovery activity.
- [You keep working harder. What wears you down is how little you get to decide.](https://clearhead.in/post-job-control-depression.html): A 2024 prospective cohort study of 5,054 employed Australian men (Taouk et al., Social Science & Medicine, Australian Longitudinal Study on Male Health, 2013-2021) found that persistent low job control was associated with about a 103 percent higher risk of later major depression symptoms compared with persistent high control, and intermittent low control with a 32 percent higher risk. This fits Karasek's 1979 demand-control model, in which the most harmful combination is high demand plus low control (a high-strain job), not high demand alone. The trap for senior professionals is that promotions add responsibility without reliably adding authority, producing responsibility without real control. Widening even a thin margin of control lowers strain.
- [You treat five hours of sleep as discipline. Your mind has been treating it as damage.](https://clearhead.in/post-sleep-mental-health.html): A 2026 population study of 318,000 U.S. adults (Ogundare, PLOS One, BRFSS 2016-2023) found adults sleeping five hours or less were about 14 percentage points more likely to be diagnosed with depression than those sleeping six to eight hours, with both short and long sleep tied to worse mental and physical health. A 2024 meta-analysis of 154 experiments (Palmer et al., Psychological Bulletin) shows losing sleep reliably lowers positive emotion and raises anxiety, so the causal arrow runs from lost sleep to low mood, not only the reverse. Short sleep worn as discipline is a measurable mental health risk.
- [You wear the stress like a badge. Your body is keeping the receipts.](https://clearhead.in/post-allostatic-load.html): A 2026 UK Biobank study of 205,504 adults (Frontiers in Cardiovascular Medicine) found a high allostatic load, the body's cumulative stress wear-and-tear score across 12 biomarkers, was associated with more than double the risk of cardiovascular disease (hazard ratio 2.15 at load 6+). A 2026 Journal of Psychosomatic Research study linked physician burnout and effort-reward imbalance to a roughly twofold higher allostatic load. Chronic work stress leaves a measurable physical mark, and recovery, sleep and close relationships lower it.
- [You think it's just a quick message. Your team reads it as the rule.](https://clearhead.in/post-after-hours-messages.html): A 2025 study by Frederik Hesse and colleagues (Journal of Occupational and Organizational Psychology, 142 companies, 23,000+ employees) found that leaders' after-hours smartphone use is linked to a shared "climate of constant connectivity" and, through it, to collective emotional exhaustion. The expectation of being reachable, more than the workload itself, is what drains people; explicit norms about availability weaken the effect.
- [You kept your job. So why does it feel this heavy?](https://clearhead.in/post-layoff-survivor-guilt.html): Layoff survivor guilt. Joel Brockner's foundational research named survivor syndrome, and the APA's 2025 Work in America survey found 54% of workers say job insecurity significantly affects their stress and 44% fear a downturn could cost them their job within a year (up from 36%). The people who keep their jobs carry guilt, ongoing dread, and a heavier workload; naming it and separating grief, fear and overload is where relief begins.
- [You built the life you were told to want. So why does it feel so flat?](https://clearhead.in/post-flourishing-research.html): The Global Flourishing Study (VanderWeele et al., Nature Mental Health 2025), a 202,898-person survey across 22 countries, found flourishing tends to be lowest in younger adulthood and does not clearly rise until around age 50, and that a nation's economic development is not positively linked to its people's sense of meaning. Success is not the same as flourishing; meaning, close relationships and character are what a demanding career crowds out.
- [The quietest burnout is the one nobody can see.](https://clearhead.in/post-quiet-cracking.html): A 2025 TalentLMS study found over half of employees are quietly cracking — delivering on the outside, eroding underneath.
- [You hold the whole team together. Who holds you?](https://clearhead.in/post-manager-burnout.html): Gallup 2025 data and a 125-study review found managers burning out faster than the people they lead.
- [You're the one who holds it together. Who holds you?](https://clearhead.in/post-holding-it-together.html): Emotional suppression and surface acting at work are linked to burnout and genuine distress.
- [You've done the work. So why do you still feel like a fraud?](https://clearhead.in/post-impostor-syndrome.html): Impostor syndrome hits high achievers hardest and doesn't respond to evidence of competence.
- [You're not burned out. You're not depressed. You're languishing.](https://clearhead.in/post-languishing.html): A 2026 national study found 61% of workers languishing in the flat, joyless middle between thriving and breaking down.
- [You built the career you wanted. So why does your 40s feel flat?](https://clearhead.in/post-mid-career-crisis.html): A 2025 University of Surrey study of 100,000+ workers found job satisfaction dips to its lowest in the 40s and recovers, but only for managers and professionals. The mid-career slump targets the people whose careers look most successful.
- [You hit every target. So why does it never feel like enough?](https://clearhead.in/post-perfectionism.html): New research splits perfectionism in two — high standards help, fear of falling short quietly harms.
- [You give more than you get back. Your mind keeps the receipt.](https://clearhead.in/post-effort-reward-imbalance.html): Three decades of effort-reward imbalance research, incl. a 2017 meta-analysis of 84,963 employees, link unrewarded effort at work to about 65% higher depression risk; a 2025 German cohort shows it accumulates over time.
- [It isn't the stress that breaks high performers. It's how they talk to themselves under it.](https://clearhead.in/post-self-compassion-work-stress.html): A 2025 longitudinal study found the same work stress predicted anxiety and depression only when self-compassion was low.
- [You rested. The exhaustion came back. Here is why.](https://clearhead.in/post-rest-burnout.html): A 2026 model argues knowledge-worker burnout is a trained mental habit, not an empty battery.
- [Your long hours have a cost your brain is quietly paying.](https://clearhead.in/post-overwork-brain.html): A 2025 brain-imaging study linked 52+ hour work weeks to structural changes in executive-function and emotion-regulation brain regions.
- [You call it juggling. Your brain is quietly paying the tax.](https://clearhead.in/post-multitasking.html): A 2025 study found multitasking raises job stress and lowers workplace wellbeing.
- [You left work hours ago. Your mind never did.](https://clearhead.in/post-cant-switch-off.html): A 2025 study tracked the mental-health cost of being unable to psychologically detach from work.
- [You are exhausted. So why are you still awake at midnight?](https://clearhead.in/post-bedtime-procrastination.html): "Revenge bedtime procrastination" — delaying sleep to reclaim time the day swallowed — and why it grips high performers.
- [That Monday dread isn't in your head. It's in your body.](https://clearhead.in/post-monday-dread.html): A 2025 study linked Monday anxiety to elevated stress hormones up to two months later.

## Articles — Money & mental health
- [The money worry isn't just stressful. It's quietly stealing your focus.](https://clearhead.in/post-money-bandwidth.html): A 2025 open-access study in Current Psychology (Esposito, 10.1007/s12144-025-08321-w) found perceived financial scarcity was associated with higher cognitive fatigue (β = 0.23), which was associated with diminished attentional control (β = -0.53) and poorer inferential learning; the driver is felt scarcity, not bank balance, so it hits high earners too. Builds on Mani et al. (2013, Science, 10.1126/science.1238041), where financial worry cut cognitive performance by roughly a full night's lost sleep, and a 2026 Frontiers in Psychology paper linking scarcity to worse risk and time decisions via weakened executive function. On the cruel loop where money worry drains the focus you need to fix it, and what helps: the Abundance Runway Calculator (a real number for the fear) and the Cognitive Load & Bandwidth Index (seeing the load).
- [You earn well. So why does money still feel unsafe?](https://clearhead.in/post-money-anxiety.html): A 2025 longitudinal study found economic insecurity harms mental health through perceived stress, not just objective numbers.
- [You make six figures. So why does it feel like survival mode?](https://clearhead.in/post-golden-handcuffs.html): A November 2025 Harris Poll found a third of six-figure earners feel stretched, struggling, or drowning — the golden-handcuffs mechanism, and what helps.
- [You out-earn most people you know. So why do you still feel behind?](https://clearhead.in/post-money-comparison.html): A 2026 Social Science & Medicine study of 200,000+ people across 22 countries found feeling poorer than peers lowers wellbeing even at the same income — relative deprivation, the salary scoreboard, and what helps.
